hook.text: The richest 1% own 46% of the world's wealth. The bottom 50% own 1%. That's 4 billion people sharing 1%.

buildup.text: Global wealth totals about $450 trillion. Half sits in the accounts and assets of 75 million people.

discovery.text: Wealth is more concentrated than income. You can earn the same salary as someone with 100x your net worth.

twist.text: Median wealth in the U.S. is $193,000. Mean wealth is $1.06 million. The average is pulled up by billionaires.

climax.text: Statistics feel abstract until you visualize: Jeff Bezos earns your lifetime salary in under 30 seconds.

punchline.text: Same planet. Different universe.

quiz.question: What share of global wealth does the bottom 50% own?

hook.text: A doctor earning $300,000 with $500,000 in student debt has a lower net worth than a janitor with a paid-off house.

buildup.text: Income is what you earn. Wealth is what you own minus what you owe. They measure different things.

discovery.text: Wealth compounds over generations. Income starts over each year. That's why wealth inequality dwarfs income inequality.

twist.text: Billionaires often report low income. They hold assets, borrow against them, and pay minimal income tax.

climax.text: Focusing only on income misses the real story. Wealth is where power, security, and opportunity actually live.

punchline.text: Income is the river. Wealth is the ocean.

quiz.question: Why is wealth inequality greater than income inequality?
options: Wealth compounds over generations while income resets yearly

hook.text: South Africa's Gini coefficient is 0.63—the highest on Earth. Denmark's is 0.28. One number captures the gap.

buildup.text: The Gini coefficient measures inequality from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person owns everything).

discovery.text: The U.S. Gini is 0.39—higher than any other developed nation. It's been rising since the 1980s.

twist.text: China's Gini went from 0.30 in 1980 to 0.47 in 2023. Rapid growth created rapid inequality simultaneously.

climax.text: Gini is imperfect—it doesn't show where the inequality is concentrated. But it's the best single number we have.

punchline.text: One number. A society's report card.

quiz.question: What does a Gini coefficient of 0 represent?

hook.text: In 2000, there were 470 billionaires worldwide. In 2024, there are 2,781. Their combined wealth: $14.2 trillion.

buildup.text: Tech created the fastest wealth accumulation in history. Bezos went from garage to $200 billion in 25 years.

discovery.text: Network effects explain it: platforms that connect billions of users create winner-take-all markets.

twist.text: During COVID, billionaire wealth grew $5 trillion while 100 million people fell into extreme poverty.

climax.text: Billionaire wealth isn't just large—it's growing faster than the economy. The gap accelerates over time.

punchline.text: The rich get richer. Literally and faster.

quiz.question: How many billionaires existed in 2000 vs 2024?

hook.text: Americans think the top 20% own 59% of wealth. The real number is 86%. People vastly underestimate inequality.

buildup.text: Harvard researcher Michael Norton asked Americans to draw their ideal wealth distribution. It looked like Sweden.

discovery.text: People support reducing inequality in principle. But they don't realize how extreme it already is.

twist.text: Both Republicans and Democrats preferred more equality than what exists. Agreement on the goal, not on the means.

climax.text: Inequality persists partly because people can't see it. The scale is literally beyond everyday comprehension.

punchline.text: The gap is bigger than you think it is.

quiz.question: How much wealth does the top 20% in America actually own?

hook.text: Between 1945 and 1975, the U.S. middle class grew, inequality shrank, and CEO-to-worker pay was 20 to 1.

buildup.text: The New Deal, strong unions, high top tax rates, and the GI Bill created the broadest prosperity in U.S. history.

discovery.text: Economists call it the Great Compression: the period when the gap between rich and poor narrowed dramatically.

twist.text: It wasn't natural. It was policy. Progressive taxes, union power, and public investment squeezed the distribution.

climax.text: The middle class didn't emerge on its own. It was built by deliberate choices that society later reversed.

punchline.text: Equality isn't default. It's designed.

quiz.question: What was the CEO-to-worker pay ratio during the Great Compression?

hook.text: Reagan cut the top tax rate from 70% to 28%. CEO pay went from 42x workers in 1980 to 399x by 2021.

buildup.text: Supply-side economics argued that cutting taxes on the rich would benefit everyone through trickle-down growth.

discovery.text: Deregulation, union-busting, and tax cuts simultaneously increased corporate power and decreased worker bargaining.

twist.text: The economy grew, but the gains went to the top. From 1979 to 2019, the top 1% captured 21% of total income growth.

climax.text: Income inequality returned to 1920s levels within 30 years. The Great Compression was systematically reversed.

punchline.text: Trickle down. Stay at the top.

quiz.question: What happened to inequality after Reagan's tax and deregulation policies?

hook.text: In 1954, 35% of U.S. workers were in a union. In 2023, 6% of private-sector workers are. Wages stagnated in between.

buildup.text: Unions gave workers collective bargaining power. They negotiated wages, benefits, and working conditions as a group.

discovery.text: Studies show union decline explains a third of the rise in male wage inequality since the 1970s.

twist.text: Globalization moved factories to countries without unions. Companies swapped expensive labor for cheaper workers.

climax.text: Without collective power, individual workers compete on price. The race to the bottom benefits employers, not employees.

punchline.text: Alone, you negotiate. Together, you demand.

quiz.question: What share of wage inequality is explained by union decline?

hook.text: In 2013, Thomas Piketty's 700-page economics book became a global bestseller. Its thesis fit one formula: r > g.

buildup.text: r is the return on capital (investments). g is economic growth. When r exceeds g, wealth concentrates at the top.

discovery.text: If investments return 5% but the economy grows 2%, capital owners pull ahead of workers every single year.

twist.text: The mid-20th century was the exception: wars, inflation, and policy briefly made g exceed r. The norm is inequality.

climax.text: Piketty showed that concentration isn't a bug—it's the default. Only intervention prevents it.

punchline.text: Capital beats labor. Math guarantees it.

quiz.question: What does r > g mean in Piketty's framework?
options: Returns on capital exceed economic growth, concentrating wealth

hook.text: Google has 92% of search. Apple took 75% of smartphone profits in 2023. Winner-take-all markets everywhere.

buildup.text: Digital platforms have zero marginal cost. Serving one million users costs barely more than serving one thousand.

discovery.text: Network effects lock users in. Everyone's on Facebook because everyone's on Facebook. Switching costs are social.

twist.text: The result: a few founders become unimaginably rich while the skilled workers who built the platforms earn salaries.

climax.text: Technology democratized access but concentrated ownership. Everyone can use Google; one company owns it.

punchline.text: Free to use. Priceless to own.

quiz.question: Why do tech platforms create winner-take-all markets?
options: Zero marginal cost and network effects lock users in

hook.text: The average person in Norway earns $87,000 per year. In Burundi, it's $240. A 362-to-1 ratio between nations.

buildup.text: Colonialism extracted wealth from the Global South for centuries. Raw materials flowed out; finished goods flowed back.

discovery.text: After independence, former colonies inherited broken institutions, arbitrary borders, and debt to former colonizers.

twist.text: Globalization helped some—China lifted 800 million from poverty—but Africa's share of global GDP has barely changed.

climax.text: Where you're born is the single largest predictor of your lifetime income. Geography is destiny.

punchline.text: Born here: opportunity. Born there: obstacle.

quiz.question: What is the biggest predictor of lifetime income?

hook.text: Gabriel Zucman estimates $7.6 trillion in personal wealth is hidden in tax havens. That's 8% of global GDP.

buildup.text: Wealthy individuals use offshore trusts, shell companies, and nominee directors to hide assets from tax authorities.

discovery.text: This hidden wealth means inequality statistics underestimate the real gap. The top is richer than we measure.

twist.text: Developing countries lose $200 billion annually to tax havens. Money that could fund schools and hospitals disappears.

climax.text: Secrecy jurisdictions exist because powerful people benefit from them. Reform needs global cooperation money resists.

punchline.text: The real numbers are hidden. On purpose.

quiz.question: How much personal wealth is estimated to be hidden in tax havens?

hook.text: A $100 Nike shoe: $2 goes to the factory worker. $5 for materials. Nike keeps $21.50 in profit.

buildup.text: Global supply chains outsource production to countries with the lowest labor costs. It keeps prices down.

discovery.text: Bangladesh garment workers earn $95/month. The Rana Plaza collapse in 2013 killed 1,134 workers in a factory.

twist.text: Economists argue sweatshop jobs are better than the alternatives in poor countries. The bar is that low.

climax.text: Consumer prices are low because labor standards elsewhere are low. Cheap clothes have a hidden human cost.

punchline.text: Your bargain is someone's poverty wage.

quiz.question: How much of a $100 Nike shoe goes to the factory worker?

hook.text: Migrant workers sent $656 billion home in 2022. That's more than all foreign aid and investment combined.

buildup.text: Remittances are money migrants send to family in their home country. It funds food, school, and housing directly.

discovery.text: India, Mexico, and the Philippines are the top recipients. For some countries, remittances are 30% of GDP.

twist.text: Transfer fees average 6%. On $656 billion, that's $39 billion in fees—mostly to banks and money transfer companies.

climax.text: Remittances fight inequality person to person. No bureaucracy, no corruption—just family helping family.

punchline.text: The world's best aid program is family.

quiz.question: How do remittances compare to foreign aid?
options: They exceed all foreign aid and investment combined

hook.text: The richest 10% produce 50% of carbon emissions. The poorest 50% produce just 12%. But climate hits the poor first.

buildup.text: Wealthy nations industrialized for 200 years using fossil fuels. Now developing nations are told to go green.

discovery.text: Climate change causes floods in Bangladesh, droughts in sub-Saharan Africa, and rising seas in Pacific islands.

twist.text: Rich countries pledged $100 billion yearly for climate adaptation. By 2022, they'd delivered less than half.

climax.text: The countries that caused the problem can afford to adapt. The countries that didn't cause it can't.

punchline.text: The polluters profit. The innocent pay.

quiz.question: What share of global carbon emissions comes from the richest 10%?

hook.text: Life expectancy in the richest U.S. neighborhoods is 87. In the poorest, it's 72. A 15-year gap by zip code.

buildup.text: Wealthy people access better food, healthcare, and housing. Poor people face pollution, stress, and untreated illness.

discovery.text: The stress of poverty itself causes disease. Chronic cortisol elevation damages the heart, immune system, and brain.

twist.text: In countries with universal healthcare, the health gap shrinks dramatically. Access matters more than medicine.

climax.text: Health inequality is wealth inequality wearing a stethoscope. Your bank account predicts your lifespan.

punchline.text: Money doesn't buy happiness. It buys years.

quiz.question: What is the life expectancy gap between rich and poor U.S. neighborhoods?

hook.text: Children of the top 1% are 77 times more likely to attend an Ivy League school than children of the bottom 20%.

buildup.text: Wealthy families invest in tutors, test prep, extracurriculars, and legacy admissions. The deck is stacked before age 5.

discovery.text: School funding tied to property tax means rich neighborhoods have better schools. Inequality funds itself.

twist.text: Even identical test scores don't equalize outcomes. Low-income high achievers attend elite colleges at half the rate.

climax.text: Education was meant to be the equalizer. Instead, it often amplifies the advantages children are born with.

punchline.text: The ladder exists. The rungs are uneven.

quiz.question: How many times more likely are top-1% children to attend Ivy League schools?

hook.text: In the 2020 U.S. election cycle, the top 100 donors gave more than the bottom 4.75 million donors combined.

buildup.text: Campaign contributions, lobbying, and think tank funding give the wealthy outsized influence over policy.

discovery.text: Princeton research found U.S. policy reflects wealthy preferences. Average citizens' views have near-zero impact.

twist.text: Citizens United (2010) allowed unlimited corporate spending on elections. Money became speech. Literally.

climax.text: Economic inequality becomes political inequality. Those with the most money shape the rules that protect their wealth.

punchline.text: One person, one vote. One dollar, one voice.

quiz.question: What did Princeton research find about U.S. policy?
options: It reflects wealthy preferences; average citizens have near-zero impact

hook.text: A child born poor in Denmark has a 15% chance of reaching the top income quintile. In the U.S., it's 7.5%.

buildup.text: Social mobility measures whether children end up richer or poorer than their parents. It's the meritocracy test.

discovery.text: The Great Gatsby Curve shows high inequality correlates with low mobility. Unequal societies stay unequal.

twist.text: Americans believe in mobility more than any developed nation—but have less of it than most European countries.

climax.text: Without mobility, inequality becomes permanent. Wealth and poverty become inherited conditions, not choices.

punchline.text: The American Dream is more real in Denmark.

quiz.question: What does the Great Gatsby Curve show?
options: High inequality correlates with low social mobility

hook.text: Countries with higher inequality have higher homicide rates. South Africa, Brazil, and Mexico top both lists.

buildup.text: When legal paths to prosperity are blocked, illegal ones open. Poverty combined with visible wealth breeds desperation.

discovery.text: Epidemiologists Wilkinson and Pickett showed inequality correlates with mental illness, drug abuse, and violence.

twist.text: Even the wealthy suffer in unequal societies: more anxiety, more security costs, less trust in public spaces.

climax.text: Inequality doesn't just harm the poor. It degrades the social fabric that everyone—rich and poor—depends on.

punchline.text: Inequality is expensive. For everyone.

quiz.question: How does inequality affect even the wealthy?
options: It increases their anxiety, security costs, and erodes trust

hook.text: The U.S. top tax rate was 91% in the 1950s. The economy boomed. Today it's 37%. Inequality boomed instead.

buildup.text: Progressive taxation takes a larger share from higher incomes. It's the most direct tool for redistribution.

discovery.text: Higher taxes on the rich funded the interstate highway system, public universities, and the space program.

twist.text: Opponents argue high taxes drive capital abroad. But during the 91% era, the U.S. had the strongest economy on Earth.

climax.text: The effective rate was never 91%—deductions brought it lower. But the signal mattered: excess wealth was taxed.

punchline.text: High rates built the middle class. Low rates shrank it.

quiz.question: What was the U.S. top tax rate during the 1950s economic boom?

hook.text: Alaska gives every resident about $1,600 per year from oil revenue. No application. No means test. Everyone gets it.

buildup.text: UBI provides a floor. Nobody falls below it. Proponents say it reduces poverty without welfare bureaucracy.

discovery.text: Stockton, California tested UBI with $500 monthly. Recipients got jobs at double the rate of the control group.

twist.text: Funding UBI for 330 million Americans at $1,000/month costs $4 trillion annually—the entire federal budget.

climax.text: UBI addresses inequality at the bottom but doesn't touch concentration at the top. It treats symptoms, not causes.

punchline.text: A floor for everyone. A ceiling for no one.

quiz.question: What happened in Stockton's UBI experiment?
options: Recipients got jobs at double the rate of the control group

hook.text: The Walton family fortune is $250 billion. Without estate tax, it passes to the next generation intact. A dynasty.

buildup.text: Estate tax takes a portion of wealth at death. The U.S. exempts the first $13 million; the rest is taxed at 40%.

discovery.text: Andrew Carnegie called inherited wealth a curse. Teddy Roosevelt pushed estate tax to prevent aristocracy.

twist.text: Trusts, foundations, and loopholes reduce effective estate tax to near zero for the wealthiest families.

climax.text: Without estate tax, wealth compounds across generations. Meritocracy gives way to inheritance as the primary path.

punchline.text: Born rich. Stay rich. Pass it on.

quiz.question: Why did Teddy Roosevelt support estate tax?
options: To prevent aristocracy from inherited wealth

hook.text: Mondragon in Spain is a worker-owned cooperative with 80,000 employees and $14 billion in revenue.

buildup.text: In cooperatives, workers own shares and vote on major decisions. Profits are shared, not extracted by shareholders.

discovery.text: Employee stock ownership plans (ESOPs) give workers equity. Companies with ESOPs have 25% higher productivity.

twist.text: Worker ownership has limits: it's hard to raise capital without outside investors, and growth can be slower.

climax.text: Ownership is the difference between earning a wage and building wealth. Workers who own share in the upside.

punchline.text: Own the company. Share the wealth.

quiz.question: What is the productivity effect of employee stock ownership plans?

hook.text: A parking lot in Manhattan is worth $100 million. The owner pays less tax than a factory employing 500 people.

buildup.text: Henry George proposed taxing land value, not improvements. Tax the location, not the building on it.

discovery.text: Land value is created by community investment—roads, schools, transit—not the owner. Society should capture that value.

twist.text: Singapore uses land value capture extensively. Public land ownership funds world-class infrastructure.

climax.text: Land value tax can't be avoided—you can't move land offshore. It's the one tax that can't be gamed.

punchline.text: Tax the land. It can't leave.

quiz.question: Why can't land value tax be avoided?
options: Land can't be moved offshore or hidden

hook.text: Goldman Sachs estimates AI could automate 300 million jobs globally. The gains flow to capital owners, not workers.

buildup.text: Previous automation displaced factory workers. AI threatens knowledge workers: lawyers, writers, analysts, coders.

discovery.text: If AI replaces labor, corporate profits soar but wages fall. The gap between capital and labor widens further.

twist.text: New technology always created new jobs before. But AI is different—it can learn and adapt faster than humans retrain.

climax.text: The question isn't whether AI creates wealth. It's whether that wealth is shared or concentrated.

punchline.text: AI creates abundance. Distribution is the question.

quiz.question: How might AI worsen wealth inequality?
options: By concentrating gains with capital owners while displacing workers

hook.text: 2.6 billion people—one-third of humanity—have no internet access. They're invisible to the digital economy.

buildup.text: The digital economy rewards connectivity. E-commerce, remote work, and fintech require internet access as a baseline.

discovery.text: In sub-Saharan Africa, only 36% are online. In Europe, it's 93%. The gap is a gateway to every other gap.

twist.text: Even in wealthy countries, rural and low-income communities lack broadband. Digital poverty exists everywhere.

climax.text: As the economy goes digital, the unconnected fall further behind. Access is the new baseline for opportunity.

punchline.text: No connection. No opportunity.

quiz.question: How many people lack internet access worldwide?

hook.text: By 2030, climate change will push 132 million more people into extreme poverty. The rich will barely notice.

buildup.text: Climate adaptation costs money: seawalls, drought-resistant crops, relocating communities. Poor nations can't afford it.

discovery.text: The green transition creates new jobs in solar, wind, and batteries—but mostly in countries that can invest.

twist.text: Lithium, cobalt, and rare earths for green tech are mined in poor countries. The pattern of extraction continues.

climax.text: Climate change and inequality reinforce each other. Solving one without the other solves neither.

punchline.text: Green for some. Brown for the rest.

quiz.question: How many additional people could face extreme poverty due to climate change by 2030?

hook.text: In 2019, 181 CEOs signed a pledge to serve all stakeholders—not just shareholders. Critics called it PR.

buildup.text: Shareholder capitalism maximizes stock price above all. Stakeholder capitalism weighs workers, communities, and planet.

discovery.text: B Corps and benefit corporations legally require balancing profit with purpose. Patagonia gave itself to a climate fund.

twist.text: Despite the pledge, CEO pay kept rising and stock buybacks hit records. Words without accountability change nothing.

climax.text: Stakeholder capitalism needs enforcement, not pledges. Voluntary goodwill doesn't survive quarterly earnings pressure.

punchline.text: Good intentions. No enforcement. Same results.

quiz.question: What happened after 181 CEOs pledged to serve all stakeholders?
options: CEO pay continued to rise and buybacks hit records

hook.text: GDP rises when someone gets cancer—treatment costs money. GDP doesn't measure well-being. It measures activity.

buildup.text: Kate Raworth's Doughnut Economics proposes measuring prosperity by whether human needs are met within planetary limits.

discovery.text: Bhutan measures Gross National Happiness instead of GDP. New Zealand budgets for well-being indicators.

twist.text: Infinite growth on a finite planet is mathematically impossible. But the entire economic system depends on it.

climax.text: Redefining success from growth to well-being would reshape every institution. That's why it's so hard to do.

punchline.text: Grow what matters. Stop counting what doesn't.

quiz.question: What does Kate Raworth's Doughnut Economics propose?
options: Meeting human needs within planetary limits
